commentary: In 2021, U.S. clothing purchasers aged 18+ had 77% online penetration before and 83% after the outbreak ends. In the U.S. 2021 chart, online penetration among grocery purchasers aged 18+ was 43% before the outbreak began and 56% after it ends. In the U.S. 2021 chart, online penetration among beauty/grooming purchasers aged 18+ was 57% before the outbreak began and 66% after it ends. During the COVID-19 outbreak, 27% of U.S. households signed up for a new paid shopping program membership. Of households that signed up for a new paid shopping program membership during the outbreak, 83% planned to keep at least one of those memberships over the next 12 months.

editorial_plan.report_thesis: The report depicts post-COVID commerce as a category-specific transition: online adoption is expected to persist unevenly, while discovery, fulfillment, retailer trial, memberships, and data sharing show distinct consumer behaviors.

themes.theme: Online penetration is projected to remain higher after the outbreak than before it across grocery, beauty/grooming, and clothing, with growth varying by category.
In car shopping, discovery and consideration have shifted online more than transactions; faster transaction adoption is tied to touchless end-to-end experiences.
Online shoppers often start at specific retailer sites or apps, with starting destinations varying by product category.
Many consumers who tried new online retailers during the outbreak plan to continue shopping with at least some of them; discovery sources vary by category.
Delivery is the most frequently used online-purchase fulfillment option across the reported categories, while grocery shoppers also use curbside and in-store pickup.
The report tracks new paid shopping memberships, plans to retain them, and household paid-membership use.
Online shoppers report differing comfort with sharing personal information and exchange some information with retailers for monetary benefits.

toc_entries.summary: A summary of the report’s main conclusions about lasting shifts in consumer shopping behavior. It highlights online adoption, car shopping, retailer discovery, purchasing from new retailers, fulfillment preferences, paid memberships, and data sharing.
key_points: Grocery, beauty/grooming, and clothing have experienced a lasting online shift; consumers aged 35+ are expected to see the largest sustained growth in online penetration.
Car shoppers have moved discovery and consideration online, while transactions are expected to shift more slowly until touchless end-to-end experiences are available.
Consumers increasingly begin online shopping at specific retailers rather than search engines; 90% or more of consumers who tried new online retailers plan to continue with at least some of them.

Delivery is the most popular fulfillment method overall, but nearly half of grocery shoppers prefer curbside or in-store pickup; more than one-quarter of households signed up for a new paid shopping membership during the outbreak.

toc_entries.summary: Examines how online shopping adoption changed during COVID-19 and how much of that change consumers expect to retain. It covers grocery, beauty/grooming, clothing, and car shopping.
key_points: Chart “Online Shopper Penetration by Product Category and Time Period,” U.S., 2021: online penetration among category purchasers was 77% for clothing, 57% for beauty/grooming, and 43% for grocery before the outbreak; after the outbreak ends, the corresponding figures are 83%, 66%, and 56% (p. 4).
The age-group charts show that grocery and beauty/grooming have the greatest projected sustained growth among older purchasers, while online clothing adoption rises across all age groups (pp. 8–10).

For car shopping, consumers have shifted discovery and consideration online more than transaction; the report identifies a touchless end-to-end experience as a prerequisite for faster online transaction adoption (pp. 11–13).

toc_entries.summary: Compares the websites and apps consumers typically visit first when shopping online across grocery, beauty/grooming, and clothing. The findings show the importance of retailer destinations and category-specific discovery habits.
key_points: Chart “First Website/App Visited When Grocery Shopping Online,” U.S., 2021: 31% of online grocery shoppers typically started at Amazon and 29% at Walmart (p. 15).
For online beauty/grooming shopping, Amazon was the most common starting point at 38% (p. 16).
For online clothing shopping, Amazon was the most common starting point at 36%; department stores accounted for 17% (p. 17).
The report’s overall conclusion is that consumers increasingly begin shopping with specific retailers rather than search engines (p. 1).

toc_entries.summary: Compares the online-purchase fulfillment option consumers use most frequently for grocery, beauty/grooming, and clothing. Delivery leads in each category, while grocery stands out for its use of pickup.
key_points: Chart “Delivery/Pickup Option Most Frequently Used for Online Purchases by Product Category,” U.S., 2021: delivery was the most frequently used option for grocery (56%), beauty/grooming (75%), and clothing (84%) (p. 19).
For grocery purchases, 34% most frequently used curbside pickup and 11% in-store pickup (p. 19).
For beauty/grooming, 11% most frequently used curbside pickup and 14% in-store pickup; for clothing, the corresponding figures were 7% and 9% (p. 19).

toc_entries.summary: Reports consumers’ experiences buying from online retailers they had not previously used, their plans to continue shopping with them, and their interest in trying additional sites and apps. It also compares how consumers discover new retailers across product categories.
key_points: Chart “Purchasing from New Websites/Apps During the COVID-19 Outbreak by Product Category,” U.S., 2021: during the outbreak, 50% of online grocery purchasers, 29% of beauty/grooming purchasers, and 35% of clothing purchasers bought from at least one new site or app; after the outbreak ends, 90%, 98%, and 97%, respectively, plan to continue shopping with at least some of these new sites or apps (p. 21).
For discovering new retailers during the outbreak, word of mouth was the top listed source for grocery (49%); social media led for beauty/grooming (53%) and clothing (49%) (p. 22).
The report finds continued interest in finding or trying new online retailers across grocery, beauty/grooming, and clothing (p. 23).

toc_entries.summary: Examines new paid shopping program sign-ups during COVID-19, households’ current paid memberships, and consumers’ plans to retain new memberships. Paid memberships are distinguished from free loyalty programs.
key_points: Chart “Signing Up for New Paid Shopping Program Memberships During the COVID-19 Outbreak,” U.S., 2021: 27% of households signed up for a new paid membership; 83% planned to keep at least one of these new memberships over the next 12 months (p. 25).

Chart “Paid Shopping Program Membership Household Penetration,” U.S., 2021: 80% of households paid for at least one membership, the average household paid for 1.7, and 64% paid for Amazon Prime (p. 27).
Half of households paid for at least one warehouse-club membership; Walmart+ had become the fourth most popular program after launching in September 2020 (p. 27).

toc_entries.section_title: Consumer Data Sharing on the Privacy-Focused Web
toc_entries.display_title: Consumer Data Sharing on the Privacy-Focused Web
toc_entries.summary: Explores what personal information online shoppers are comfortable sharing with retailers in exchange for personalized experiences and monetary benefits. It also describes common data-sharing behaviors tied to rewards and discounts.
key_points: Chart “Average Number of Personal Data Types … Comfortable Sharing,” U.S., 2021: the average online shopper was comfortable sharing 6.3 types of personal data to create a retailer account or profile in exchange for personalized benefits (p. 30).

Consumers were more comfortable sharing demographic details than sensitive or behavioral information; for example, 78% were comfortable sharing gender, compared with 35% for browsing/search history on a website or app (p. 31).

Chart “Sharing of Personal Data with Online Retailers in Exchange for Monetary Benefits,” U.S., 2021: 67% had signed up for a retailer email list for a welcome reward, 57% had shared their date of birth for a birthday reward, 66% had joined a loyalty program for rewards, and 32% had signed up for a retailer credit card for rewards (p. 32).

toc_entries.summary: Describes Activate Consulting’s growth-oriented capabilities and its implementation and program-management support. The report also includes the Activate Consulting Team credit in its closing material.
key_points: The capabilities overview lists growth strategy, consumer insights and segmentation, digital strategy, salesforce effectiveness, strategic due diligence and value creation for private equity investors, pricing, and marketing optimization (p. 36).
Implementation and program management are presented as supporting execution of strategy and performance-improvement initiatives (p. 36).

Compares the websites and apps consumers typically visit first when shopping online across grocery, beauty/grooming, and clothing. The findings show the importance of retailer destinations and category-specific discovery habits. Chart “First Website/App Visited When Grocery Shopping Online,” U.S., 2021: 31% of online grocery shoppers typically started at Amazon and 29% at Walmart (p. 15). For online beauty/grooming shopping, Amazon was the most common starting point at 38% (p. 16). For online clothing shopping, Amazon was the most common starting point at 36%; department stores accounted for 17% (p. 17). The report’s overall conclusion is that consumers increasingly begin shopping with specific retailers rather than search engines (p. 1).

eCommerce discovery has forever changed as most consumers are starting their online shopping journey with specific retailers instead of search engines.

report_context.title: The Post-COVID Online Shopper: New Challenges and Opportunities
report_context.overview: The Post-COVID Online Shopper: New Challenges and Opportunities An Activate Viewpoint presenting findings from Activate’s May 2021 consumer technology and media research (n = 2,913) on online shopping behavior and expectations after COVID-19. It covers shifts in online adoption across product categories, car shopping, retailer discovery, delivery and pickup, new online retailers, paid shopping memberships, and consumers’ willingness to share data for personalized or monetary benefits. Consumer research on post-COVID online shopping, covering adoption across auto, grocery, beauty/grooming, and clothing, as well as e-commerce discovery, delivery versus pickup, new online retailers, shopping memberships, and consumer data sharing. The geographic coverage is the U.S.; the research is framed around 2021 and shopping before, during, and after the COVID-19 outbreak, defined as beginning in March 2020.
methods: Large-scale consumer research examined post-COVID online shopping across auto, grocery, beauty/grooming, and clothing.
Analysis used the Activate COVID-19 Consumer Tech & Media Study, fielded May 2021 (n = 2,913); the report identifies the analysis as Activate analysis.

Online-shopping penetration measures are reported for U.S. consumers aged 18+ who purchase in the relevant product category at least once per year. For online grocery shoppers, the report defines eligibility as having shopped for groceries online since the COVID-19 outbreak began in March 2020.

sections.summary: A summary of the report’s main conclusions about lasting shifts in consumer shopping behavior. It highlights online adoption, car shopping, retailer discovery, purchasing from new retailers, fulfillment preferences, paid memberships, and data sharing.
key_points: Grocery, beauty/grooming, and clothing have experienced a lasting online shift; consumers aged 35+ are expected to see the largest sustained growth in online penetration.
Car shoppers have moved discovery and consideration online, while transactions are expected to shift more slowly until touchless end-to-end experiences are available.
Consumers increasingly begin online shopping at specific retailers rather than search engines; 90% or more of consumers who tried new online retailers plan to continue with at least some of them.
